quality_rationale: Concrete and well-designed: specific sites and elevation range, a defined sampling window, a named analytical method (micro-FTIR), explicit contamination controls (procedural and field blanks), and a clean hypothesis distinguishing regional from long-range sources via back-trajectory modelling. It states significance and commits to open data. Weaknesses: only six sites limits statistical power and generalisability, and the 10-micrometre lower cut-off excludes the most abundant and arguably most health-relevant small particles, which the abstract acknowledges but does not mitigate.
title: Quantifying Microplastic Deposition in Alpine Snow
artefact:
Microplastics are now found from the deep ocean to remote mountains, but the rate at which they deposit onto high-altitude snow remains poorly quantified. We propose to measure microplastic deposition across an elevation gradient in the European Alps and to identify the dominant transport pathway.

Over two winter seasons we will collect fresh-snow cores at six sites spanning 1,200 to 3,000 metres, sampling within 48 hours of snowfall to capture discrete deposition events. Samples will be filtered in a clean-air cabinet to limit contamination, and particles between 10 and 500 micrometres will be quantified and chemically identified using micro-Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy. Procedural blanks and field blanks will bound background contamination, the chief weakness of earlier studies.

We will test whether deposition flux declines with altitude, which would indicate regional sources, or stays flat, which would point to long-range atmospheric transport. Back-trajectory modelling of air masses for each snowfall will link measured fluxes to likely source regions.

The significance is twofold. First, alpine snow feeds rivers that supply drinking water to millions, so quantifying deposition is a first step towards assessing exposure. Second, the elevation gradient offers a natural test of transport mechanism that bulk sampling cannot provide. Limitations include the small site count and the lower size cut-off of 10 micrometres, below which our method cannot reliably detect particles. The dataset and protocols will be released openly to support comparison across mountain regions.
